title: Conjunctions
shortDescription: The joining words that link ideas — coordinating, subordinating, and correlative pairs that must always come in twos.
genZNote: Conjunctions are relationship counsellors for clauses — they decide if two ideas are equals, or if one depends on the other.

rows: and, but, or, nor, for, yet, so (FANBOYS)
Joins two equal/independent clauses or words
because, although, since, if, when, while, unless
Joins a dependent clause to a main clause
either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also, both...and
Work in pairs to join balanced elements

sections.heading: Correlative conjunctions — the matching-pair rule
bullets: Correlative conjunctions must be followed by grammatically PARALLEL structures: 'She is not only intelligent but also hardworking' (adjective matches adjective), not 'not only intelligent but also she works hard.'
'Either...or' and 'neither...nor' pair options — with 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the NEARER subject: 'Neither the teacher nor the students WERE ready' (were agrees with 'students').
Never mix correlative pairs: 'either...nor' or 'neither...or' are incorrect — 'either' pairs only with 'or', 'neither' pairs only with 'nor'.

sections.heading: Subordinating conjunction traps
bullets: 'Although'/'though' should not be paired with 'but' in the same sentence — 'Although he was tired, he continued working' (not 'Although he was tired, BUT he continued').
'Because' should not be paired with 'so' in the same sentence for the same reason — pick one connector, not both, to avoid redundancy.
'Unless' already means 'if not' — saying 'unless...not' creates a double negative: 'Unless you don't hurry' is often wrong; it should be 'Unless you hurry.'

sections.heading: Common linking/transition words (a light layer above conjunctions)
sections.body: Words like 'however', 'therefore', 'moreover', 'nevertheless', and 'consequently' are conjunctive adverbs, not true conjunctions — they connect ideas in meaning but need a semicolon or full stop before them when joining two independent clauses, not just a comma: 'It was raining; however, we continued the match' (semicolon, not comma, before 'however').

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Conjunctions join words, phrases, or clauses — coordinating (equal ideas), subordinating (dependent on a main clause), or correlative (matched pairs).
keyFacts: FANBOYS = for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so — the coordinating conjunctions.
Correlative pairs (either/or, neither/nor, not only/but also) must never be mixed and must join parallel structures.
Don't double up 'although...but' or 'because...so' in one sentence.

highYieldFacts: 'Not only...but also' requires parallel grammatical structure on both sides.
With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
commonTraps: Writing 'Although he tried hard, but he failed' — redundant conjunction pairing.
mustRemember: Check both sides of a correlative conjunction for matching grammatical form.
possibleQuestions: Spot the error: 'He is neither intelligent nor he is hardworking.' (should be 'nor hardworking' to keep parallel structure)
